notes.text: You hold the pawn with b5, ready to push b4 if White challenges it with a4.
This is the Alekhine variation, which tends to lead to highly tactical and complicated positions.
Your queen guards b7 and steps out of the way; Stockfish likes this most, and strong players choose it.
Your bishop develops with the Czech variation and eyes the center, making it harder for White to play e4.
Your knights are happy and e4 is hard for White, though the bishop on c4 eyes f7.
White can exchange on d5, which makes your g6 less useful than a6 would be.
White's e4 is the Geller Gambit, another possible try.
The Chebanenko prepares b5 and makes developing your light bishop easier.
White's queen eyes f5, so skip Bf5 and Bg4; play g6, dxc4 or e6 instead.
White prepares to push the e-pawn to e4.
White castles to unpin the knight and prepares to push e4.
Avoid ...Bf5 here: White takes on d5 and plays Qb3, winning a pawn.
White develops with Bf4 and pins your e5 knight to the queen, which is its only defender.
The Slav keeps your light bishop free to roam instead of locked behind pawns, as it is after e6.
Challenging the e5 knight with your b8 knight is the main move.
This is White's main line.
This is the Exchange Variation: White is slightly better because your light bishop has trouble developing.
You can win the e4 pawn, but it isn't free: White gets a big initiative.
This was once the main line, but White has scored very well against it.
White's bishop takes the c4 pawn back, so material is level again.
White exchanges the central pawns, and you retake with your knight.
This odd-looking move heads for a Semi-Slav setup and usually gives up c4; Carlsen played it.
This is the Chameleon Variation, a viable line for Black that this study skips.
This is the main line: you allow e4 and hope to defend against White's attack, with the knight later helping from f8.
White's e3 keeps the center stable and hopes you overextend your queenside pawns.
This is the position you want: meet every Qb3 with Qb6 and learn to play queenless middlegames.
White grabs a big share of the center and space.
Your knight hits the c3 knight, forcing White to trade or push it away with e4.
You push the e-pawn to fight for the center and free your dark-squared bishop.
These two moves define the Slav: solid, but developing your light bishop is hard and White can target your queenside pawns.
This move defines the Semi-Slav: you threaten to take on c4 and defend it with b5.
White threatens e4 with a tempo on your bishop, and a quick kingside attack follows if you allow it.
Semi-Slav with Bg5: you choose between taking on c4 or chasing the bishop with h6. Both are sharp.
The game is very sharp and complicated and needs more analysis to play properly.
The Winawer Countergambit gives up a pawn for quicker development, but you usually fall behind after regaining it.
Your knight retakes the pawn and hits the loose knight on c4, leaving White few options.
Castling gives you the option of Bg6 next, which stops White's e4 push.
White avoids the sharp Slav and wants Bf4 then e3; you can seek tactics with an early Qb6.
The main move: let White take on c4, then bring your knight to b6 or push e5.
A side line for another study; it can transpose back into the Exchange or Main Line.
Protect the c4 pawn with your b-pawn.
In the Sokolov system your knight aims to trade off White's active knight on c4.
White gains queenside space; you often fianchetto your dark bishop to hit White's center.
Bf4 is White's most common move: it develops the bishop and delays Nf3.
Your c4 pawn is hanging again, and playing e6 would concede the center.
White wants to win back the c4 pawn with the bishop.
Another variation you might see.
Your knight lands on a nice square at d5, supported by the c6 pawn.
White prepares e4, which you cannot stop, so you must play for piece activity.
White gave up the dark bishop, so you keep the bishop pair.
White has the full center; if you simply castle, you are back in the main line.
White's fianchetto setup with g3 is the main continuation.
White chases your light bishop; this pawn frees your dark bishop and lets you retake on f5.
This is the usual Pure Slav position: you counter the center and press on the b6-f2 diagonal.
Playing e6 here looks fine, but White's kingside initiative with g4 makes it a poor choice.
This is another candidate move for White.
Don't recapture on b5 right away, or you lose a pawn and maybe more.
Retreating the bishop argues White's knight is misplaced, but in practice Black scores poorly here.
Your a-pawn defends b5, so Nxb5 is not a worry.
This is the Dutch variation: White opens the bishop to recapture the c4 pawn.
Nc6 often transposes, but it lets White play e4, which Nf6 would have prevented.
This position is very playable for you, with real winning chances.
After you retake on e5, you hold the bishop pair, but White gets compensation by stopping queenside castling.
Grabbing on b5 is a mistake: after cxb5 and Qf3, your Qc7 and Bb7 trap White's queen.
This may look like it keeps both pawns defended, but it also runs into problems.
This line is tricky: played carelessly, you can lose quickly, so know the theory well.
Your bishop pins the f3 knight, so White's e4 would lose a pawn to a capture on f3 and queen takes d4.
Your pawn shoos the queen away from h5.
White will win the c4 pawn back eventually, but you gain time to develop your pieces.
White enters the Exchange Variation, which can be tricky for you to play.
The e3 pawn boxes in White's dark bishop, and opening the center early can turn this calm line sharp.
White backs d4 and discourages taking on c4, steering you toward Semi-Slav or Chebanenko setups.
White's queen adds pressure on your d5 pawn, so keep it defended.
Black often answers with e6, the traditional Queen's Gambit Declined.
White's a4 stops your b5, so you can't easily hold c4, but you gain time to develop.
Your c-pawn hits d4 and guards your b4 pawn; a5 is also fine but rarer.
White is following his plan of retaking the center with e4.
You will answer with ...c5 to keep the balance in the center.
Your e5 pawn hits d4 to bust open the center.
Nc3 stops Bf5, so your best reply is e6, transposing into the Semi-Slav.
The knight looks odd on c1, but it is heading for the fine b3 square.
White keeps e4 free for the knight, controls the center and prepares to take on c4.
White's knight hits your queen, and the b7 pawn is attacked too, so you must defend it.
Your knight heads for the weak b4 square; playable, but it can be tricky.
White takes the pawn back and avoids the complications of e4; the line branches after you castle.
This is one possible continuation in the main line.
Your knight occupies e4 itself, blocking White's pawn and offering a trade; beware the rare g4 attack.
Completing the exchange is your best option; you accept a symmetrical position and avoid Qxd5.
White can also play the knight to h4, going after your bishop and transposing into the Bled attack.
Your bishop pins the knight on f3 to the queen.
White has a good grip on the center; a good plan is Bh5, pinning the knight.
White hits your b4 pawn twice, so your a-pawn adds a defender at once.
White wants to win the c4 pawn back with tempo, but with no pin on e6 yet, Bg5 isn't a threat.
White shouldn't grab the d5 pawn right away; instead it builds up pressure on it.
White takes on e5, a common choice; follow this line next.
Developing the bishop before the knight looks natural, but it makes your life hard.
White's pawn asks your bishop to decide: take on f3, or retreat to h5.
Retreating the bishop stops e4 tactically: White's e4 would no longer come with a tempo.
Your queen develops to c7 to prepare the e5 push, likely leading to the Carlsbad.
The first Slav problem is solved: your light bishop is out on its most active diagonal.
This is occasionally seen and usually transposes back to the lines with ...Nf6.
Your advanced c-pawn will soon fall, leaving you with weak isolated pawns.
You head for Semi-Slav style play, with your light bishop temporarily shut behind the pawn chain.
Your bishop pressures the c3 knight and takes control of e4, preparing a bishop sacrifice there.
The exchange variation releases the tension early and gives you equality, though it is hard to win.
You have lots of fun moves coming; at the highest level Black is having a good time here.
Taking the pawn leaves you slightly worse according to the engine; see why next.
Your e6 pawn closes the position and gives you a solid structure with normal-looking moves.
Your knight on d7 stops White's knight from jumping to e5 and chasing your bishop.
Trade queens with check and simplify the game.
White's knight hits your bishop, transposing to the Bled attack and aiming for the bishop pair.
Your queen takes the bishop on c1 with check, and it is checkmate.
White simply recaptures the c-pawn with the bishop.
The quiet Breyer: White usually plays slowly and aims for a Catalan-like setup with g3.
This is the main move, and you now have three main replies in the Slav.
White has a strong centralized knight and you are undeveloped, so this is not fun to play.
Your setup is solid, but White's bishop can take your knight on a6 and wreck your pawn structure.
White grabs central space, but the c3 knight loses e4 as a retreat square.
The Semi-Slav keeps your bishop inside the pawns for now, ready to free it with c5 or e5.
Your knight can't move, so Nfd7 adds a second defender to the pinned knight.
Your a-pawn eyes b4; you hope to use the weak squares on b4 and d5, though your queenside looks awkward.
You take the gambit pawn; ...b5 can hold it, since White's c3 knight is exposed to ...b4.
The Steiner variation is viable but harder; you should know the theory well.
This is the main reply; don't fear doubled f-pawns, since you have time for it.
White's knight wants to reach b4 eventually, and you should not allow that.
Your queen guards both pawns at once, but this turns out to be a mistake.
The Bled attack is White's chief sideline: the knight goes after your light-squared bishop before winning back c4.
Your knight hits the c4 knight, and White usually retreats rather than trading.
White chooses now: e5 is the sharpest and most played, d5 is calmer, while castling or Bg5 are worse.
A solid but rare option; it usually transposes to the Chebanenko main line.
Your a-pawn stops the knight and b4. Later prepare c5 with knight, rook and queen moves.
You have the bishop pair and should be happy.
White prepares Bf4 to pressure the e5 square and a fianchetto of the light bishop.
White releases the central tension, and play usually transposes into exchange Slav lines.
Your knight eyes e4. If White plays Bf4 or Bg5, take on c4 and keep the pawn.
Your knight is best here: it controls e4 and protects the d5 pawn.
Your knight heads for b4, where pawns can't chase it away after White's a4.
Your knight challenges White's knight on e5; e6, Bb4 and castling come next.
The Boor attack is a rare try: White prepares e4 but weakens f2, and Qb6 is your best reply.
Your bishop keeps an eye on e4, so White must protect the pawn or push it.
Two White pieces hit b4, so you add another defender with a5.
This is the main reply, but your d5 pawn is weak.
White grabs the center, so your b5 pawn holds on to c4 and expands on the queenside.
Your bishop hits the f3 knight, which could jump to e5, a weak square for you.
This move order is inaccurate: you can develop your bishop outside the pawns and equalize.
The e5 pawn attacks your knight on f6; how do you save it?
White's g3 prepares the bishop fianchetto again.
White's queen pressures your knight on b6 and the awkward queenside.
Trade the knights first, before recapturing on b5.
White's knight eyes your c4 pawn to win it back, and b5 can't defend it.
White's knight threatens both your bishop and the hanging c4 pawn.
Your c4 pawn takes the b3 square away from White's queen.
Developing the bishop now is still too early, for the same reasons as before.
White's a4 hits your b5 pawn to break up your queenside; you can answer with b4.
The position is equal.
Your bishop pins the c3 knight against the king, on a square pawns can't kick it from.
A simple defence: your second knight now protects the pinned knight on e5.
Your bishop pins the f3 knight, which makes the e5 break possible and eyes the d4 pawn.
This is the most popular and best move; your weakened kingside means you usually castle queenside.
If White grabs the g5 pawn, your knight takes on c4 and you win a piece.
Your bishop pins the f3 knight to the queen, and White will want to break the pin soon.
You can retake with the queen or castle long; both work well.
Moving this knight to d7 runs into Nxf7, which gives White a crushing attack in practice.
White has won the pawn back; now you have two main replies.
Your queen defends the c3 pawn and the loose bishop on a6.
Always take on c4 when you can: the queen was guarding that pawn, so you lose no time.
White adds pressure on d5 and stops your bishop going to f5.
The thematic e6 is back; from here the main moves are common, though other lines exist.
Bb7 is more precise than Be7: it prepares against a painful Ne5 from White.
White's knight eyes d4 and e5; this is the main line and gives you many replies.
This is the usual continuation for White here.
You get your light bishop out, and the f6 knight keeps Qb3 from forking b7 and d5.
The usual reply opens your dark-squared bishop and lets your e-pawn recapture if White takes on f5.
Your bishop defends the c4 pawn.
Your b5 pawn guards the c4 pawn, so White must fight to win it back.
White defends the e4 pawn and threatens e5 to trade off the light-squared bishops.
White exchanges early; recapture on d5 and the symmetrical position is equal and often drawn.
White protects the bishop and prepares e4 eventually.
In the Alekhine Variation, White's bishop is opened up to threaten your c4 pawn.
A rich middlegame: what matters is understanding the Slav ideas so you reach positions you know.
White's pawn hits your bishop; the main answer is to sacrifice it on e4 for three pawns.
White's queen hits b7, so you must give up the center with dxc4 or play e6.
You get a happy pawn structure, with your b5 and c4 pawns linked.
White's a4 stops you supporting the c4 pawn with b5 and weakens b4, but develops nothing.
Just defend: your b-pawn guards the c4 pawn.
White develops the bishop and prepares to castle short; you usually answer with f6 or g5.
Your knight prepares a pawn break with b6 or e5 against White's space advantage.
Developing the knight is best in the Slav; you can also play e6 for the Semi-Slav.
White's queen guards c4 and stops your bishop from reaching f5.
You take the pawn and plan to develop your light bishop while White is busy recapturing.
White's bishop pins your e5 knight to your queen, but it's less scary than it looks.
White puts the knight back in the center and declines the trade; this is the main line.
White finally takes over the centre with e5, hitting your knight with tempo.
Your bishop harasses the f3 knight, but it isn't pinned, so White's Ne5 hits the bishop with tempo.
Your queen defends the b7 pawn, which is the common reply.
Your far-advanced queenside pawns are like mini queens; White will try to go around them and attack your king.
The Schlechter Variation aims for a King's Indian type of structure.
Spooky: White threatens Qxf7, which would be checkmate. Push your g-pawn to chase the queen.
Your queen escapes the attack and protects b7, while you threaten to win a loose piece.
Retaking on d5 right away is a blunder: your queen takes the bishop on c1 with checkmate.
White has the extra tempo, but your position is very playable.
White's knight jumps to e5 to chase your light-squared bishop.
Retreating looks odd, but it is a way to aim for a draw or beat a stronger player.
This is the Wiesbaden: you prepare Bb4, where White's a4 pawn leaves your bishop undisturbed.
Bb4 is more sound than Be7: it is active, and White's a-pawn cannot kick it away.
Your b-pawn now defends the c4 pawn.
White's pawn hits your bishop and the d5 pawn, a threat like the one before.
White prepares e4, and you have no real way to prevent it.
White simply develops the knight to its natural square, pressuring your d5 pawn.
With a4, White gave up the e4 square for a while; your bishop develops naturally and you stand well.
The structure looks odd, but you keep the bishop pair, and White's queenside has weaknesses too.
You fianchetto the dark bishop and back up f5 so your light bishop can develop.
This typical Exchange Slav position is calmer and less rich than the main lines, but still gives you good ideas.
Both b5 and Nbd7 are common, viable answers to this odd-looking move.
This rare Lasker variation aims your knight at the b4 outpost instead of your dark-squared bishop.
In the Czech Variation you use your time to develop the light bishop to f5, the best square.
White gets a big center, but your solid position keeps that space edge from being decisive.
White stops your b5, but that lets you fight for the center with e5; Black tends to do well.
This is the main line. It can look scary, as the knight eyes e6, f7 and h7.
Your bishop adds protection to e6, just in case White tries something there.
You are a pawn up but cramped, while White has kingside attacking chances; you play on the queenside.
This keeps your bishop pair and your grip on e4, so White can't build a full center.
Nc3 is White's most promising reply: it develops actively and adds pressure on d5.
This is the Pure Slav: you plan ...b5 to keep the extra pawn and give your light bishop room.
Nf3 is the second most common move and allows a completely equal position, often chosen for a draw.
Your knight escapes with check, and White's king cannot go forward.
White's bishop checks you, and only one reply is really playable.
You head for a kingside fianchetto, with the bishop going to g7.
White fianchettos and will castle next, but you have an annoying reply.
This is yet another candidate move for White.
White has a broad center, but you are a pawn up.
White's knight challenges your best kingside defender and eyes c5, a square you don't want to give up.
White's a-pawn stops your b5, which would have backed up the c4 pawn.
The old mainline: your pawn defends the pinned knight on e5.
White's knight jumps to the center to win back the c4 pawn, a sharp and ambitious try.
White's knight is stifling; find the only move that doesn't blow up your position.
White's e3 looks like a harmless developing move, but your ninth move needs care.
White recaptures on c4. You can now enter the Carlsbad with your queen on c7.
Or you can reroute your knight to b6 instead.
White develops and eyes e5. Avoid ...Bf5 and ...dxc4 here; you have two main replies.
Your bishop sidesteps the discovered attack and pins the f3 knight against the queen.
This main move lets White take on c4 and prepares your knight for b6 or the e5 push.
White reroutes the knight to b3 and still plans e4.
The Schlechter prepares to fianchetto your dark-squared bishop.
You dream of Qc7 and c5, trading light bishops and targeting White's light squares.
You play e6 almost every time, preparing your bishop for b4, a square weakened by a4.
You protect the c4 pawn with b5; if White wins it back, White should be better.
Your queen and knight both watch e5, so the white knight can't return there.
An odd line you may meet: White spends an extra move putting a knight on the edge.
Very sharp: your king is still in the center, but your bishops and the g-file give real kingside chances.
White closes your bishop's diagonal, but your c4 pawn is still hanging.
White's e4 pawn hits your bishop with tempo, and you can retreat it to g6 or g4.
White's knight attacks your bishop on f5, planning to exchange it after you take on f4.
Na2 is also seen, hitting your b-pawn right away.
The knight move looks silly but isn't: White is a pawn down and must attack, so careful with h6.
This is White's strongest move here; other moves give White little counterplay.
White's queen hits both your b7 and d5 pawns, and b7 looks shaky.
White's g3 doesn't challenge the c4 pawn; you can defend with b5, g6 or Nbd7.
Developing the knight is White's main response.
The Slav supports your center with the c-pawn, so your light bishop stays free.
Your e5 pawn keeps fighting for the center by hitting the d4 pawn.
Your knight overprotects the d5 pawn and develops the kingside; now White must show a plan.
This knight move is also possible, but it will most likely transpose back into the main line.
In the Slav gambit White takes the centre while you expand on the queenside.
With e6, your bishop defends the b-pawn, but you give up the c-pawn.
Your a-pawn stops White's a4-a5 push and controls b4 as a possible outpost.
Your bishop checks the king, gaining time to save your knight efficiently.
Recommended: take on c4 when a queen or bishop can guard it, or play e6 for Semi-Slav positions.
White defends c4 and frees the light bishop, but blocks in the c1 bishop; e6, Bf5 or Bg4 all work.
Like in the Semi-Slav, activate your light-square bishop and defend your overextended b-pawn.
Your pawn attacks the bishop on f4, so White must decide how to respond.
White simply develops the g1 knight; this is an uncommon move.
Everything is defended: your knight on d5 and the pawn on c4 are both covered.
Instead of just losing the bishop pair, White's knight hits your bishop on f5 in return.
Pro games have reached this position; White continues with e4 or Rd1.
White adds another attacker on your c3 pawn.
